direct_claims: This chart shows annual death rates for females at six ages—0, 10, 25, 45, 65, and 80—from 1933 to 2023, expressed per 1,000 people of a given age.
The comparison covers the World, India, the United States, and Japan.
The chart belongs to the demography and public health domain.
It was published by Our World in Data and cites the Human Mortality Database and the UN World Population Prospects as sources.
In demography, an age-specific death rate measures the probability of dying within a year for people at a particular age, summarized here as deaths per 1,000 females of that age.
Because the evidence comes from the image alone, precise values, exact turning points, and causes of fluctuations should be treated as approximate unless confirmed by the underlying dataset.
derived_claims: Across all six age panels, death rates generally decline over time in all four geographies. — derived by reading broad downward trends across all panels.
Japan appears to have some of the lowest recent death rates in several adult and older-age panels. — derived by comparing line endpoints across panels.

India starts from notably higher death rates than the United States and Japan in multiple age groups, especially in mid-century portions of the series. — derived by comparing relative line levels across panels and years.

Looking at separate age panels is important because mortality risk differs greatly across the life course, with infancy and old age usually having much higher death rates than childhood or young adulthood. — derived by comparing value ranges across age panels.
The large long-run declines at age 0 are consistent with major reductions in infant mortality. — derived by reading the strong downward trend in the 0-years panel.
The broad downward trends suggest that female survival improved substantially over the period shown. — derived by reading long-run declines across all panels.

The chart is structured to allow comparison both across time and across ages, which helps distinguish whether mortality improvement was concentrated in childhood, adulthood, or old age. — derived from the multi-panel age layout.

Some panels show short-term spikes or irregularities rather than perfectly smooth decline, indicating that mortality can be affected by temporary shocks as well as long-run improvement. — derived by reading local fluctuations and spikes in several panels.
